9	# Feishu Document Formatting
10	
11	## Core contract
12	
13	Format by visible content and semantic role, then mutate the **smallest complete structural block** in document order. An MCP success response is not completion; each completed mutation batch must survive read-back with tables, code, diagrams, media, and neighbors intact.
14	
15	User-explicit styling overrides defaults. Content skills decide facts; this skill controls serialization, layout, update safety, and verification.
16	
17	## Required reference
18	
19	Read [formatting rules](references/formatting-rules.md) before every write.
20	
21	## Workflow
22	
23	### 1. Fetch and classify
24	
25	Choose create, append/insert, restyle one block, replace one section, or repair malformed rich text. For an existing document, call `fetch_doc` without `limit`/`offset` to get the complete document, then locate boundaries locally. Use pagination only when the user explicitly requests it; in that case continue until the complete target block and both neighbors are available. Never infer current headings/tokens from an old draft.
26	
27	### 2. Build the structural manifest
28	
29	In document order record headings; table boundaries/shape; fenced code and Mermaid boundaries; callout/grid/container boundaries; whiteboard/image/file tokens, order, and neighbors; and target/preserve status. Do not split a table/fence/container or cross unrelated media.
30	
31	### 3. Allocate auditable widths
32	
33	Table total width matches the document's **actual text-column width**, verified so it does not overflow the adjacent callout/heading: wide-mode docs ≈ 930px, classic/narrow docs ≈ 800px. Width count equals column count and width sum equals the chosen total.
34	
35	- tiny enum/index: 70–100;
36	- status/date/version: 90–140;
37	- numeric before/after/delta: 105–145;
38	- symbol/API: 150–220;
39	- repo/code path/revision: 210–300;
40	- explanation/evidence/root cause: remaining 280–500.
41	
42	Center headers and compact values; for a user-requested uniform-centered style, center **all** cells with equal columns summing to the text width. Leave paths/prose left-aligned by omitting `align`. Vertical centering (垂直居中) is not settable via the update tool — it is a Feishu UI action (select table → 垂直居中); never claim it from a write. If the text width is insufficient for readability, split by question.
43	
44	### 4. Preflight serialization
45	
46	Check canonical same-block bold; alignment outside emphasis; balanced table/row/cell structure; equal cell count per row; balanced code/Mermaid fences; blank-line separation; container support; and punctuation locale consistency (CJK context → full-width marks, pure-ASCII context → ASCII mark + space, no mixing, code/ASCII fences exempt). Fenced code in an enhanced table cell is allowed only when its complete nested syntax has been intentionally validated; Mermaid/media/nested tables are not inserted into cells. Never write a fetched `<whiteboard token="..."/>` as creation syntax.
47	
48	### 5. Mutate in document order
49	
50	Policy for existing documents: no `overwrite` or `replace_all`. Use one unique complete-block `replace_range`; `selection_by_title` only for the exact fetched section; precise insert modes for adjacency; append only at the true end. If `selection_with_ellipsis` includes literal `...`, escape it as `\.\.\.`. Process the earliest remaining target first; one section per batch is the long-report default.
51	
52	### 6. Resolve asynchronous completion
53	
54	A mutation returning `task_id` is not a completed batch. Poll the same create/update tool with `task_id` until success/failure. Only then fetch and validate. Never begin another mutation while the preceding batch is pending.
55	
56	### 7. Enforce the read-back barrier
57	
58	After every completed batch, fetch the affected complete block and neighbors. Verify content/order; table shape/width count/sum; alignment; bold; code/Mermaid fences/language/order; container boundaries; media token/order/neighbors; warnings; and unrelated content. On failure, stop and repair only the smallest failed block, then re-run the barrier.
59	
60	## Hard rules
61	
62	- No existing-document `overwrite`/`replace_all` under this safety policy.
63	- No non-unique selection or speculative broadening.
64	- No split structural block or unrelated media crossing.
65	- No table width that overflows the document text column; match the verified text-column width (≈800 narrow, ≈930 wide).
66	- No claim that vertical centering was applied via a write (it is UI-only).
67	- No width-count/sum mismatch.
68	- No blanket centering of paths/prose.
69	- No mixed punctuation locales: CJK-context punctuation is full-width, pure-ASCII-context punctuation is ASCII + space; applies to all marks, never inside code/ASCII fences.
70	- No next batch before async completion and read-back pass.
71	- No rendering-success claim from MCP acceptance alone.
72	
73	## Final gate
74	
75	After all batch barriers, full-fetch and compare the initial manifest plus intended changes. Confirm headings, tables, fences, links, containers, media/neighbors, and warnings. Markdown read-back does not by itself prove visual font weight or final bitmap rendering; state that limit.

43	If 960px cannot remain readable, split by reader question. Exceed 960 only when the user explicitly overrides the default. A one-off compact/equal-width/all-left request also overrides defaults without changing future defaults.

45	Examples (930px):
46	- `类型/版本/说明`: `130,150,650`
47	- `状态/Change/路径/说明`: `110,140,270,410`
48	- `指标/前/后/变化/来源/解释`: `180,115,115,110,100,310`
49	
50	### Uniform-centered style (common user request)
51	
52	When the user asks for「表格总宽度 = 文本宽度、文本水平居中」or an equivalent uniform look: use **equal columns** summing to the text width and set `{align="center"}` on **every** cell (header and data). Equal-split examples — 800px: 5-col `160,160,160,160,160`, 4-col `200,200,200,200`, 3-col `266,267,267`, 2-col `400,400`; 930px: 5-col `186×5`, 4-col `232,233,232,233`, 3-col `310,310,310`.
53	
54	### Alignment
55	
56	Center headers and compact values with `{align="center"}`; center **all** cells for the uniform-centered style. Omit `align` for left-aligned paths/prose. Put attributes outside bold. Do not emit `{align="left"}`.
57	
58	**Vertical centering (垂直居中) cannot be set through the MCP/markdown update tool** — `{align=...}` controls horizontal alignment only. Vertical alignment is a table-cell property applied in the Feishu UI (select the table → cell alignment → 垂直居中). Never claim vertical centering was applied by a write; report it as a one-click UI follow-up.
59	
60	## lark-table structure
61	
62	Hierarchy is `lark-table → lark-tr → lark-td`; each row has equal cells; cell content has surrounding blank lines; do not mix pipe-table syntax or nest lark-tables.
63	
64	Enhanced cells may contain complex content such as a fenced code block when the complete nested structure is intentionally generated and validated. Keep ordinary technical-report code blocks outside tables by default for readability. Do not place Mermaid, media, or another lark-table inside a cell.
65	
66	## Bold safety
67	
68	Use paired same-block `**text**`, no inner whitespace/newline, no escaping when emphasis is intended, no split delimiters, and no changes inside code. Repair the smallest complete paragraph/list/callout/cell; never run a document-wide regex.
69	
70	## Punctuation locale consistency
71	
72	Match every punctuation mark to its surrounding language and never mix locales within one run. This applies to **all** punctuation (colon, comma, period, semicolon, enumeration comma `、`, brackets, quotes, exclamation/question marks, ellipsis, dash), not only colons.
73	
74	- CJK context (both sides CJK, or at least one adjacent side is CJK): use full-width CJK punctuation — `：，。；、！？（）【】「」《》…——` — with no trailing ASCII space.
75	- Pure Latin/ASCII context (both sides are English words, numbers, code tokens, or identifiers): use the ASCII mark followed by a single space — `: ` `, ` `; ` `. ` — never a full-width mark.
76	- Never mix inside one clause: `实测结论:即` → `实测结论：即`; `codec-only,parser` → `codec-only, parser`; a Chinese sentence must not delimit clauses with ASCII `,`/`;`, and an all-English list must not use `，`/`；`.
77	- Do not alter punctuation inside fenced code blocks or ASCII diagrams — full-width marks are wider and break monospace alignment, and code content must stay byte-exact. Normalize prose, headings, callouts, blockquotes, and table cells only.
78	- When normalizing, edit the smallest unique block and reproduce the surrounding text (especially comment-anchored spans) exactly, so comment anchors are not orphaned.
79	
80	## Fence and container safety
81	
82	- Preserve matching fence and language labels.
83	- A selection contains the complete fence/container or none of it.
84	- Compare fence count, language, first/last content line, and order after each batch.
85	- Keep Mermaid/code outside callouts.
86	- Mermaid conversion warnings are failures to investigate.
87	
88	## Selection safety
89	
90	- `selection_by_title` replaces the complete heading section; use only after fetching and confirming that scope.
91	- `selection_with_ellipsis` boundaries should use 10–20 unique characters.
92	- Literal `...` in source must be escaped as `\.\.\.`.
93	- `insert_after` uses the matched range end; `insert_before` uses its start.
94	- Non-unique selection is a stop condition, not a reason to broaden across media.
95	
96	## Ordered asynchronous batches
97	
98	1. Fetch the complete document by default (or user-requested pages) and build the manifest.
99	2. Number targets by current document order.
100	3. Mutate the earliest complete block.
101	4. If a `task_id` returns, poll the same tool until terminal success/failure; pending is not completion.
102	5. Fetch the complete affected block and neighbors.
103	6. Validate content, table shape/width/alignment, bold, fences, containers, media, warnings, and unrelated content.
104	7. Only after PASS mutate the next block.
105	8. Finish with a full fetch and manifest comparison.
106	
107	One section per batch is the long-report default. Split oversized sections only at heading/complete-block boundaries.
108	
109	## Red flags
110	
111	- existing-document overwrite/replace_all;
112	- pending task followed by another mutation or early fetch;
113	- non-unique or media-crossing selection;
114	- width count/sum mismatch, or an unverified fixed width that overflows/underfills the document text column;
115	- claiming vertical centering was set by a write (it is UI-only);
116	- blanket-centered path/prose;
117	- broken fence/container;
118	- next batch before read-back;
119	- changed media/fence/table count without intent;
120	- MCP acceptance treated as rendered success.

2	name: diagram-first-documentation
3	author: JUSTiceMaMo
4	version: "1.0"
5	created: 2026-08-20
6	description: Use when turning fragmented engineering notes, diffs, logs, measurements, or existing documents into newcomer-readable technical documentation for code review, debugging or incident review, implementation walkthroughs, feature handoff, validation closure, or technical decisions.
7	---
8	
9	# Diagram-first Documentation
10	
11	## Core principle
12	
13	Organize around the reader's questions, not the author's chronology. Use diagrams only where they compress structure or causality better than prose, while keeping every claim tied to evidence.
14	
15	**Two task shapes.** (a) Author a new document from raw notes/diffs/logs. (b) **Convert** an existing document's flat prose or tables into diagrams on request (e.g. "文字不生动，绘制图形表示原理和流程"). In conversion mode: preserve the existing facts, exact labels, and neighbouring rich content; change only the targeted block into the visual that fits its information shape (see the two-step encoding decision in diagram-selection); add at most one takeaway; and do not let the new diagram duplicate an adjacent one.
16	
17	**A diagram reads as authoritative, so precision matters more than in prose.** Never let a visual encode a vague, guessed, or unverified condition, threshold, or step—a hand-wavy branch label such as "size ok?" is a defect, not decoration. Every node, edge, and label must be copied from evidence, derived from it and marked as interpretation, or shown as unknown. Converting prose into a picture must not smuggle in a fact the evidence does not state; if a real condition is fuzzy, make it precise from the source (e.g. "compile-time flag on?") or mark it unknown.
18	
19	## Workflow
20	
21	### 1. Fix the goal and scope
22	
23	Identify the audience, review goal, supplied evidence, desired output, and publication target. If a missing audience or goal would materially change the document, ask one focused question; otherwise assume a technical newcomer preparing to review.
24	
25	Do not add operations, hardening, ownership, rationale, tests, or lifecycle behavior absent from the inputs, and do not expand the result into full API or source documentation. Include unsupported ideas only when the user requests recommendations or an unresolved decision requires them; then keep them in a short **Follow-up** section labeled as proposals.
26	
27	### 2. Inventory evidence
28	
29	Classify important statements before drafting:
30	
31	| Class | Use for |
32	|---|---|
33	| **Fact** | Direct observations from source, diffs, logs, measurements, or document content |
34	| **Interpretation** | Explanations supported by facts but not raw evidence |
35	| **Decision** | Chosen action, trade-off, or review conclusion |
36	| **Limit** | Unknown, untested path, or boundary beyond which the conclusion does not apply |
37	
38	Never smooth uncertainty into fact. Keep rejected hypotheses distinguishable from the supported explanation.
39	
40	### 3. Map reader questions and classify source complexity
41	
42	Select only questions that serve the stated goal, in this order when relevant:
43	
44	1. What happened or changed?
45	2. Where is it in the larger system?
46	3. How does the important mechanism work?
47	4. What changed, and what deliberately stayed unchanged?
48	5. What evidence supports the conclusion?
49	6. What remains unknown or outside scope?
50	7. What decision or next action follows?
51	
52	Each section and diagram must answer one of these questions. Remove material that answers none.
53	
54	Before drafting, build an internal coverage map for every selected question:
55	
56	```text
57	reader question → supporting evidence → best visual → exact-value table, if needed → limiting evidence
58	```
59	
60	Classify the input by **independent information layers**, not raw length:
61	
62	- **Short or single-mechanism note:** one main chain plus a compact proof or boundary. Use the concise path.
63	- **Long or multi-stage handoff:** several distinct layers—such as system position, transformation stages, before/after structure, performance or memory causality, experiment isolation, and validation closure—where collapsing a layer would break traceability. Use the deep handoff path.
64	
65	When a long engineering source is requested as a document “for others” or for newcomers and no narrower goal is supplied, default to a newcomer-readable **technical handoff**, not an executive summary. Do not mistake a concise prompt for a request to discard supplied technical layers.
66	
67	### 4. Build the terminology ladder before technical wording
68	
69	Introduce specialized concepts as:
70	
71	```text
72	plain-language meaning → technical term → exact source/code label
73	```
74	
75	Example: `two read positions → input cursors → pa / pb`.
76	
77	Use a plain-language title and opening where possible. For a Chinese long-form deep technical document, name the deliverable with **“深度梳理”**—for example, `主题：机制、部署与性能归因深度梳理`. Do not use **“交接”** or **“技术交接”** in the document title; keep `handoff` only as an internal workflow classification, not reader-facing naming. If the user explicitly supplies a title, preserve it unless they ask for renaming. If the conclusion needs an unfamiliar term, place the terminology key immediately after the title and before the conclusion. Expand every acronym at its first appearance, including conclusions, tables, and diagram labels. Put the key before the first technical sentence or visual that depends on unfamiliar protocol, metric, operation, or component terms; include all nouns used by the first diagram, not only acronyms.
78	
79	After drafting, scan from the first line downward and verify that each specialized term is defined before that occurrence. Keep exact function, field, event, instruction, and file names for deep review, but make the plain-language meaning primary. Add a legend only when colors, line styles, symbols, or abbreviations carry meaning.
80	
81	### 5. Choose one evidence-backed visual per question
82	
83	Read [references/diagram-selection.md](references/diagram-selection.md) for type selection, complexity-sensitive visual budgets, density, legends, and generic Mermaid **and plaintext text-sketch** patterns.
84	
85	**Two visual encodings are equally canonical**: rendered diagrams (Mermaid) and inline **plaintext text-sketches** — ASCII box/arrow/lane drawings inside a fenced code block. When a principle or flow is currently written as prose or a plain table and reads as "not vivid" (文字不生动), convert it to a diagram rather than leaving it as text: use **Mermaid** for flow/sequence/state that benefits from rendering, and a **text-sketch** when you need precise inline annotations, parallel-lane / SIMD layout, memory/buffer layout, an AND-intersection funnel, a compact state machine, or role/ownership labels running alongside the flow — or when platform rendering is unreliable and you want copy-pasteable monospace. A table stays a table only for exact parallel values or mappings; a table that actually encodes order, causality, transformation, or layout is a signal to convert it.
86	
87	- For a short or single-mechanism note, use **1–3 core diagrams** according to distinct evidence-backed questions; one diagram is enough when the source supports only one visual question.
88	- For a long or multi-stage handoff, let distinct reader questions determine the count; **4–7 non-duplicative diagrams is typical, not a quota**. Keep up to the first 2–3 in the one-minute path and place supporting proof, attribution, decision, or validation visuals in deep review.
89	- Do not convert a process, causal chain, transformation, experiment-isolation boundary, decision path, or validation loop into a table merely because earlier diagrams already consumed a numeric budget. Use tables for exact comparisons, mappings, and compact evidence lookup.
90	
91	Give each mechanism or causal chain one canonical visual. For a system interaction or feature handoff, the primary interaction diagram must span every participant named in the requested scope, including asynchronous consumers and delivery components. A secondary diagram is justified only when it answers a different reader question, such as lifecycle failure, resource causality, comparison validity, or proof closure. Do not pair a sequence diagram and flowchart for the same chain.
92	
93	Preserve the evidence-backed **intermediate states** required to understand a conclusion. If a conclusion depends on several transformations or causal steps, a start→end summary is insufficient; show those steps or mark the unavailable link as unknown. Split crowded visuals by reader question instead of deleting the states that carry the explanation.
94	
95	Each node, edge, destination, responsibility, and edge label must be copied from the input or clearly labeled as interpretation. Do not enrich a request with likely payload details or insert a likely event channel. If a destination or owner is unknown, show the boundary as unknown or omit it.
96	
97	Add at most one takeaway after a diagram, and only when it contributes information the labels alone do not provide. Omit it when the labels already carry the point.
98	
99	### 6. Compose to a proportional reading budget
100	
101	- **10 seconds:** title and one-sentence conclusion or purpose.
102	- **1 minute:** up to the first 2–3 core diagrams, each with at most one useful takeaway, plus an explicit change/result boundary.
103	- **Deep review:** additional distinct visuals, source map, exact evidence, commands or values, decisions, and limits.
104	
105	For short source notes, impose **no word-count or diagram minimum**. Use **1–3 diagrams** according to the evidence-backed questions, and keep a **900-word ceiling** unless the user requested depth or omission would lose supplied evidence. Evidence-rich short notes commonly land around **600–850 words**, but tiny one-question inputs should remain substantially shorter. Remove repeated takeaways, generic cautions, undefined side concepts, and redundant checklists first.
106	
107	For long or multi-stage handoffs, do **not** impose the short-note word or diagram ceiling. Keep the one-minute path independently scannable, then spend deep-review space in proportion to the independent questions and supplied evidence. Added length must come from useful visual layers, exact evidence, boundaries, or decisions—not arrow-by-arrow narration, repeated conclusions, or prose padding. In a process-heavy handoff, diagrams should normally be at least as numerous as tables; treat a table-heavy draft as a signal to re-check whether a process or causal chain was flattened into rows.
108	
109	Useful default shapes are:
110	
111	```text
112	Short note:
113	Plain-language title → terminology → conclusion → 1–3 evidence-backed core visuals → evidence and limits
114	
115	Long handoff:
116	Plain-language title → terminology → one-minute visual path → deep mechanism/transformation visuals
117	→ exact comparison tables → attribution and experiment boundaries → validation closure and limits
118	```
119	
120	Treat each important point and quantitative value as having one primary home. After the canonical causal visual, do not add an “at a glance” chronology that walks the arrows again. An evidence table should map claims to evidence, not reconstruct the sequence. A key boundary may appear in the conclusion, one diagram, and one evidence or limit statement; do not restate it in every takeaway, checklist, and section.
121	
122	### 7. Produce the canonical document first
123	
124	Write platform-neutral Markdown. The canonical visual source is Mermaid for rendered diagrams and fenced plaintext text-sketches (ASCII) for inline principle/flow drawings; both are platform-neutral and survive without an image round-trip. Separate product behavior, measurement instrumentation, and validation assets whenever they coexist; state only the supplied role and do not infer deployment or shipping status from a test or profile path.
125	
126	Preserve source ambiguity instead of resolving it. Do not infer that one branch ran merely because another did not, convert a tested dimension into a supported boundary, or complete missing ownership and data destinations from typical architecture. Attribute conclusions to the evidence that directly proves them—for example, a byte comparison proves byte identity while a matching hash only corroborates it.
127	
128	Use the source's exact metric name and scope: `502 rate = 0` does not become “failure rate = 0.” Avoid comparative claims such as “smallest,” “only,” or “all” unless the supplied evidence establishes the comparison set. Do not infer behavior of successful or unobserved cases from an intermittent failure description.
129	
130	Do not add claims about rendering, deployment, authorization, ownership, unchanged responsibilities, verification steps, request contents, or data destinations unless they were actually checked or supplied. Label necessary interpretation as interpretation.
131	
132	Only adapt or publish to Feishu when requested. Before doing so, read [references/feishu-adapter.md](references/feishu-adapter.md). Default to draft and preview, not silent publication.
133	
134	## Final gate
135	
136	Before delivery, apply every objective gate in [references/readability-gates.md](references/readability-gates.md). Revise failed gates rather than hiding them with more prose; if a gate cannot be verified, state the corresponding limit.

9	# Feishu Document Formatting
10	
11	## Core contract
12	
13	Format by visible content and semantic role, then mutate the **smallest complete structural block** in document order. An MCP success response is not completion; each completed mutation batch must survive read-back with tables, code, diagrams, media, and neighbors intact.
14	
15	User-explicit styling overrides defaults. Content skills decide facts; this skill controls serialization, layout, update safety, and verification.
16	
17	## Required reference
18

20	
21	## Workflow
22	
23	### 1. Fetch and classify
24	
25	Choose create, append/insert, restyle one block, replace one section, or repair malformed rich text. 26	
27	### 2. Build the structural manifest
28	
29	In document order record headings; table boundaries/shape; fenced code and Mermaid boundaries; callout/grid/container boundaries; whiteboard/image/file tokens, order, and neighbors; and target/preserve status. Do not split a table/fence/container or cross unrelated media.
30	
31	### 3. Allocate auditable widths
32	
33	Table total width matches the document's **actual text-column width**, verified so it does not overflow the adjacent callout/heading: wide-mode docs ≈ 930px, classic/narrow docs ≈ 800px. Width count equals column count and width sum equals the chosen total.
34	
35	- tiny enum/index: 70–100;
36	- status/date/version: 90–140;
37	- numeric before/after/delta: 105–145;
38	- symbol/API: 150–220;

40	- explanation/evidence/root cause: remaining 280–500.
41

Leave paths/prose left-aligned by omitting `align`. Vertical centering (垂直居中) is not settable via the update tool — it is a Feishu UI action (select table → 垂直居中); never claim it from a write. If the text width is insufficient for readability, split by question.
43	
44	### 4. Preflight serialization
45	
46	Check canonical same-block bold; alignment outside emphasis; balanced table/row/cell structure; equal cell count per row; balanced code/Mermaid fences; blank-line separation; container support; and punctuation locale consistency (CJK context → full-width marks, pure-ASCII context → ASCII mark + space, no mixing, code/ASCII fences exempt). Fenced code in an enhanced table cell is allowed only when its complete nested syntax has been intentionally validated; Mermaid/media/nested tables are not inserted into cells. Never write a fetched `<whiteboard token="..."/>` as creation syntax.
47	
48	### 5. Mutate in document order
49	
50	Policy for existing documents: no `overwrite` or `replace_all`. Use one unique complete-block `replace_range`; `selection_by_title` only for the exact fetched section; precise insert modes for adjacency; append only at the true end. If `selection_with_ellipsis` includes literal `...`, escape it as `\.\.\.`. Process the earliest remaining target first; one section per batch is the long-report default.
51	
52	### 6. Resolve asynchronous completion
53	
54	A mutation returning `task_id` is not a completed batch. Poll the same create/update tool with `task_id` until success/failure. Only then fetch and validate. Never begin another mutation while the preceding batch is pending.
55	
56	### 7. Enforce the read-back barrier
57	
58	After every completed batch, fetch the affected complete block and neighbors. Verify content/order; table shape/width count/sum; alignment; bold; code/Mermaid fences/language/order; container boundaries; media token/order/neighbors; warnings; and unrelated content. On failure, stop and repair only the smallest failed block, then re-run the barrier.
59	
60	## Hard rules
61	
62	- No existing-document `overwrite`/`replace_all` under this safety policy.
63	- No non-unique selection or speculative broadening.
64	- No split structural block or unrelated media crossing.
65	- No table width that overflows the document text column; match the verified text-column width (≈800 narrow, ≈930 wide).
66	- No claim that vertical centering was applied via a write (it is UI-only).
67	- No width-count/sum mismatch.
68	- No blanket centering of paths/prose.
69	- No mixed punctuation locales: CJK-context punctuation is full-width, pure-ASCII-context punctuation is ASCII + space; applies to all marks, never inside code/ASCII fences.
70	- No next batch before async completion and read-back pass.
71	- No rendering-success claim from MCP acceptance alone.
72	
73	## Final gate
74	
75	After all batch barriers, full-fetch and compare the initial manifest plus intended changes. Confirm headings, tables, fences, links, containers, media/neighbors, and warnings. Markdown read-back does not by itself prove visual font weight or final bitmap rendering; state that limit.

Equal-split examples — 800px: 5-col `160,160,160,160,160`, 4-col `200,200,200,200`, 3-col `266,267,267`, 2-col `400,400`; 930px: 5-col `186×5`, 4-col `232,233,232,233`, 3-col `310,310,310`.
53	
54	### Alignment
55	
56	Center headers and compact values with `{align="center"}`; center **all** cells for the uniform-centered style. Omit `align` for left-aligned paths/prose. Put attributes outside bold. Do not emit `{align="left"}`.
57	
58	**Vertical centering (垂直居中) cannot be set through the MCP/markdown update tool** — `{align=...}` controls horizontal alignment only. Vertical alignment is a table-cell property applied in the Feishu UI (select the table → cell alignment → 垂直居中). Never claim vertical centering was applied by a write; report it as a one-click UI follow-up.
59	
60	## lark-table structure
61	
62	Hierarchy is `lark-table → lark-tr → lark-td`; each row has equal cells; cell content has surrounding blank lines; do not mix pipe-table syntax or nest lark-tables.
63	
64	Enhanced cells may contain complex content such as a fenced code block when the complete nested structure is intentionally generated and validated. Keep ordinary technical-report code blocks outside tables by default for readability. Do not place Mermaid, media, or another lark-table inside a cell.
65	
66	## Bold safety
67	
68	Use paired same-block `**text**`, no inner whitespace/newline, no escaping when emphasis is intended, no split delimiters, and no changes inside code. Repair the smallest complete paragraph/list/callout/cell; never run a document-wide regex.
69	
70	## Punctuation locale consistency
71	
72	Match every punctuation mark to its surrounding language and never mix locales within one run. This applies to **all** punctuation (colon, comma, period, semicolon, enumeration comma `、`, brackets, quotes, exclamation/question marks, ellipsis, dash), not only colons.
73	
74	- CJK context (both sides CJK, or at least one adjacent side is CJK): use full-width CJK punctuation — `：，。；、！？（）【】「」《》…——` — with no trailing ASCII space.
75	- Pure Latin/ASCII context (both sides are English words, numbers, code tokens, or identifiers): use the ASCII mark followed by a single space — `: ` `, ` `; ` `. ` — never a full-width mark.
76	- Never mix inside one clause: `实测结论:即` → `实测结论：即`; `codec-only,parser` → `codec-only, parser`; a Chinese sentence must not delimit clauses with ASCII `,`/`;`, and an all-English list must not use `，`/`；`.
77	- Do not alter punctuation inside fenced code blocks or ASCII diagrams — full-width marks are wider and break monospace alignment, and code content must stay byte-exact. Normalize prose, headings, callouts, blockquotes, and table cells only.
78	- When normalizing, edit the smallest unique block and reproduce the surrounding text (especially comment-anchored spans) exactly, so comment anchors are not orphaned.
79	
80	## Fence and container safety
81	
82	- Preserve matching fence and language labels.
83	- A selection contains the complete fence/container or none of it.
84	- Compare fence count, language, first/last content line, and order after each batch.
85	- Keep Mermaid/code outside callouts.
86	- Mermaid conversion warnings are failures to investigate.
87	
88	## Selection safety
89	
90	- `selection_by_title` replaces the complete heading section; use only after fetching and confirming that scope.
91	- `selection_with_ellipsis` boundaries should use 10–20 unique characters.
92	- Literal `...` in source must be escaped as `\.\.\.`.
93	- `insert_after` uses the matched range end; `insert_before` uses its start.
94	- Non-unique selection is a stop condition, not a reason to broaden across media.
95	
96	## Ordered asynchronous batches
97	
98	1. Fetch the complete document by default (or user-requested pages) and build the manifest.
99	2. Number targets by current document order.
100	3. Mutate the earliest complete block.
101	4. If a `task_id` returns, poll the same tool until terminal success/failure; pending is not completion.
102	5. Fetch the complete affected block and neighbors.
103	6. Validate content, table shape/width/alignment, bold, fences, containers, media, warnings, and unrelated content.
104	7. Only after PASS mutate the next block.
105	8. Finish with a full fetch and manifest comparison.
106	
107	One section per batch is the long-report default. Split oversized sections only at heading/complete-block boundaries.
108	
109	## Red flags
110	
111	- existing-document overwrite/replace_all;
112	- pending task followed by another mutation or early fetch;
113	- non-unique or media-crossing selection;
114	- width count/sum mismatch, or an unverified fixed width that overflows/underfills the document text column;
115	- claiming vertical centering was set by a write (it is UI-only);
116	- blanket-centered path/prose;
117	- broken fence/container;
118	- next batch before read-back;
119	- changed media/fence/table count without intent;
120	- MCP acceptance treated as rendered success.

1	---
2	name: diagram-first-documentation
3	author: JUSTiceMaMo
4	version: "1.0"
5	created: 2026-08-20
6	description: Use when turning fragmented engineering notes, diffs, logs, measurements, or existing documents into newcomer-readable technical documentation for code review, debugging or incident review, implementation walkthroughs, feature handoff, validation closure, or technical decisions.
7	---
8	
9	# Diagram-first Documentation
10	
11	## Core principle
12	
13	Organize around the reader's questions, not the author's chronology. Use diagrams only where they compress structure or causality better than prose, while keeping every claim tied to evidence.
14	
15	**Two task shapes.** (a) Author a new document from raw notes/diffs/logs. (b) **Convert** an existing document's flat prose or tables into diagrams on request (e.g. "文字不生动，绘制图形表示原理和流程"). In conversion mode: preserve the existing facts, exact labels, and neighbouring rich content; change only the targeted block into the visual that fits its information shape (see the two-step encoding decision in diagram-selection); add at most one takeaway; and do not let the new diagram duplicate an adjacent one.
16	
17	**A diagram reads as authoritative, so precision matters more than in prose.** Never let a visual encode a vague, guessed, or unverified condition, threshold, or step—a hand-wavy branch label such as "size ok?" is a defect, not decoration. Every node, edge, and label must be copied from evidence, derived from it and marked as interpretation, or shown as unknown. Converting prose into a picture must not smuggle in a fact the evidence does not state; if a real condition is fuzzy, make it precise from the source (e.g. "compile-time flag on?") or mark it unknown.
18	
19	## Workflow
20	
21	### 1. Fix the goal and scope
22	
23	Identify the audience, review goal, supplied evidence, desired output, and publication target. If a missing audience or goal would materially change the document, ask one focused question; otherwise assume a technical newcomer preparing to review.
24	
25	Do not add operations, hardening, ownership, rationale, tests, or lifecycle behavior absent from the inputs, and do not expand the result into full API or source documentation. Include unsupported ideas only when the user requests recommendations or an unresolved decision requires them; then keep them in a short **Follow-up** section labeled as proposals.
26	
27	### 2. Inventory evidence
28	
29	Classify important statements before drafting:
30	
31	| Class | Use for |
32	|---|---|
33	| **Fact** | Direct observations from source, diffs, logs, measurements, or document content |
34	| **Interpretation** | Explanations supported by facts but not raw evidence |
35	| **Decision** | Chosen action, trade-off, or review conclusion |
36	| **Limit** | Unknown, untested path, or boundary beyond which the conclusion does not apply |
37	
38	Never smooth uncertainty into fact. Keep rejected hypotheses distinguishable from the supported explanation.
39	
40	### 3. Map reader questions and classify source complexity
41	
42	Select only questions that serve the stated goal, in this order when relevant:
43	
44	1. What happened or changed?
45	2. Where is it in the larger system?
46	3. How does the important mechanism work?
47	4. What changed, and what deliberately stayed unchanged?
48	5. What evidence supports the conclusion?
49	6. What remains unknown or outside scope?
50	7. What decision or next action follows?
51	
52	Each section and diagram must answer one of these questions. Remove material that answers none.
53	
54	Before drafting, build an internal coverage map for every selected question:
55	
56	```text
57	reader question → supporting evidence → best visual → exact-value table, if needed → limiting evidence
58	```
59	
60	Classify the input by **independent information layers**, not raw length:
61	
62	- **Short or single-mechanism note:** one main chain plus a compact proof or boundary. Use the concise path.
63	- **Long or multi-stage handoff:** several distinct layers—such as system position, transformation stages, before/after structure, performance or memory causality, experiment isolation, and validation closure—where collapsing a layer would break traceability. Use the deep handoff path.
64	
65	When a long engineering source is requested as a document “for others” or for newcomers and no narrower goal is supplied, default to a newcomer-readable **technical handoff**, not an executive summary. Do not mistake a concise prompt for a request to discard supplied technical layers.
66	
67	### 4. Build the terminology ladder before technical wording
68	
69	Introduce specialized concepts as:
70	
71	```text
72	plain-language meaning → technical term → exact source/code label
73	```
74	
75	Example: `two read positions → input cursors → pa / pb`.
76	
77	Use a plain-language title and opening where possible. For a Chinese long-form deep technical document, name the deliverable with **“深度梳理”**—for example, `主题：机制、部署与性能归因深度梳理`. Do not use **“交接”** or **“技术交接”** in the document title; keep `handoff` only as an internal workflow classification, not reader-facing naming. If the user explicitly supplies a title, preserve it unless they ask for renaming. If the conclusion needs an unfamiliar term, place the terminology key immediately after the title and before the conclusion. Expand every acronym at its first appearance, including conclusions, tables, and diagram labels. Put the key before the first technical sentence or visual that depends on unfamiliar protocol, metric, operation, or component terms; include all nouns used by the first diagram, not only acronyms.
78	
79	After drafting, scan from the first line downward and verify that each specialized term is defined before that occurrence. Keep exact function, field, event, instruction, and file names for deep review, but make the plain-language meaning primary. Add a legend only when colors, line styles, symbols, or abbreviations carry meaning.
80	
81	### 5. Choose one evidence-backed visual per question
82	
83	Read [references/diagram-selection.md](references/diagram-selection.md) for type selection, complexity-sensitive visual budgets, density, legends, and generic Mermaid **and plaintext text-sketch** patterns.
84	
85	**Two visual encodings are equally canonical**: rendered diagrams (Mermaid) and inline **plaintext text-sketches** — ASCII box/arrow/lane drawings inside a fenced code block. When a principle or flow is currently written as prose or a plain table and reads as "not vivid" (文字不生动), convert it to a diagram rather than leaving it as text: use **Mermaid** for flow/sequence/state that benefits from rendering, and a **text-sketch** when you need precise inline annotations, parallel-lane / SIMD layout, memory/buffer layout, an AND-intersection funnel, a compact state machine, or role/ownership labels running alongside the flow — or when platform rendering is unreliable and you want copy-pasteable monospace. A table stays a table only for exact parallel values or mappings; a table that actually encodes order, causality, transformation, or layout is a signal to convert it.
86	
87	- For a short or single-mechanism note, use **1–3 core diagrams** according to distinct evidence-backed questions; one diagram is enough when the source supports only one visual question.
88	- For a long or multi-stage handoff, let distinct reader questions determine the count; **4–7 non-duplicative diagrams is typical, not a quota**. Keep up to the first 2–3 in the one-minute path and place supporting proof, attribution, decision, or validation visuals in deep review.
89	- Do not convert a process, causal chain, transformation, experiment-isolation boundary, decision path, or validation loop into a table merely because earlier diagrams already consumed a numeric budget. Use tables for exact comparisons, mappings, and compact evidence lookup.
90	
91	Give each mechanism or causal chain one canonical visual. For a system interaction or feature handoff, the primary interaction diagram must span every participant named in the requested scope, including asynchronous consumers and delivery components. A secondary diagram is justified only when it answers a different reader question, such as lifecycle failure, resource causality, comparison validity, or proof closure. Do not pair a sequence diagram and flowchart for the same chain.
92	
93	Preserve the evidence-backed **intermediate states** required to understand a conclusion. If a conclusion depends on several transformations or causal steps, a start→end summary is insufficient; show those steps or mark the unavailable link as unknown. Split crowded visuals by reader question instead of deleting the states that carry the explanation.
94	
95	Each node, edge, destination, responsibility, and edge label must be copied from the input or clearly labeled as interpretation. Do not enrich a request with likely payload details or insert a likely event channel. If a destination or owner is unknown, show the boundary as unknown or omit it.
96	
97	Add at most one takeaway after a diagram, and only when it contributes information the labels alone do not provide. Omit it when the labels already carry the point.
98	
99	### 6. Compose to a proportional reading budget
100	
101	- **10 seconds:** title and one-sentence conclusion or purpose.
102	- **1 minute:** up to the first 2–3 core diagrams, each with at most one useful takeaway, plus an explicit change/result boundary.
103	- **Deep review:** additional distinct visuals, source map, exact evidence, commands or values, decisions, and limits.
104	
105	For short source notes, impose **no word-count or diagram minimum**. Use **1–3 diagrams** according to the evidence-backed questions, and keep a **900-word ceiling** unless the user requested depth or omission would lose supplied evidence. Evidence-rich short notes commonly land around **600–850 words**, but tiny one-question inputs should remain substantially shorter. Remove repeated takeaways, generic cautions, undefined side concepts, and redundant checklists first.
106	
107	For long or multi-stage handoffs, do **not** impose the short-note word or diagram ceiling. Keep the one-minute path independently scannable, then spend deep-review space in proportion to the independent questions and supplied evidence. Added length must come from useful visual layers, exact evidence, boundaries, or decisions—not arrow-by-arrow narration, repeated conclusions, or prose padding. In a process-heavy handoff, diagrams should normally be at least as numerous as tables; treat a table-heavy draft as a signal to re-check whether a process or causal chain was flattened into rows.
108	
109	Useful default shapes are:
110	
111	```text
112	Short note:
113	Plain-language title → terminology → conclusion → 1–3 evidence-backed core visuals → evidence and limits
114	
115	Long handoff:
116	Plain-language title → terminology → one-minute visual path → deep mechanism/transformation visuals
117	→ exact comparison tables → attribution and experiment boundaries → validation closure and limits
118	```
119	
120	Treat each important point and quantitative value as having one primary home. After the canonical causal visual, do not add an “at a glance” chronology that walks the arrows again. An evidence table should map claims to evidence, not reconstruct the sequence. A key boundary may appear in the conclusion, one diagram, and one evidence or limit statement; do not restate it in every takeaway, checklist, and section.
121	
122	### 7. Produce the canonical document first
123	
124	Write platform-neutral Markdown. The canonical visual source is Mermaid for rendered diagrams and fenced plaintext text-sketches (ASCII) for inline principle/flow drawings; both are platform-neutral and survive without an image round-trip. Separate product behavior, measurement instrumentation, and validation assets whenever they coexist; state only the supplied role and do not infer deployment or shipping status from a test or profile path.
125	
126	Preserve source ambiguity instead of resolving it. Do not infer that one branch ran merely because another did not, convert a tested dimension into a supported boundary, or complete missing ownership and data destinations from typical architecture. Attribute conclusions to the evidence that directly proves them—for example, a byte comparison proves byte identity while a matching hash only corroborates it.
127	
128	Use the source's exact metric name and scope: `502 rate = 0` does not become “failure rate = 0.” Avoid comparative claims such as “smallest,” “only,” or “all” unless the supplied evidence establishes the comparison set. Do not infer behavior of successful or unobserved cases from an intermittent failure description.
129	
130	Do not add claims about rendering, deployment, authorization, ownership, unchanged responsibilities, verification steps, request contents, or data destinations unless they were actually checked or supplied. Label necessary interpretation as interpretation.
131	
132	Only adapt or publish to Feishu when requested. Before doing so, read [references/feishu-adapter.md](references/feishu-adapter.md). Default to draft and preview, not silent publication.
133	
134	## Final gate
135	
136	Before delivery, apply every objective gate in [references/readability-gates.md](references/readability-gates.md). Revise failed gates rather than hiding them with more prose; if a gate cannot be verified, state the corresponding limit.
137

1	# Diagram Selection
2	
3	Choose a visual by the **shape of the information**, not by domain or by a favorite template. One diagram answers one primary reader question.
4	
5	## Selection table
6	
7	| Information shape / reader question | Preferred form | Keep out of it |
8	|---|---|---|
9	| Nested calls: where is the relevant code reached? | Call-flow diagram | Data values and timing detail |
10	| Ordered interaction across components: who sends what, and when? | Sequence diagram | Internal implementation of every participant |
11	| Branching logic: what decisions produce each outcome? | Flowchart | A linear numbered narrative |
12	| Transformation or movement: how does data change through stages? | Data-flow or pipeline diagram | Unrelated ownership boundaries |
13	| Change boundary: what changed and what stayed stable? | Before/after or boundary view | Full source-code reproduction |
14	| Lifecycle: which states and transitions are valid? | State diagram | Unordered feature lists |
15	| Mapping: which item corresponds to which source, owner, or result? | Compact table | Dozens of parallel diagram nodes |
16	| Proof: how does evidence close a claim? | Verification flow plus evidence table | Unsupported conclusion text |
17	| Parallelism: how are elements processed in parallel (SIMD lanes, batching)? | Text-sketch (lane diagram) | Per-element narration |
18	| Memory / buffer layout: what occupies which region, what is reused? | Text-sketch (layout diagram) | Byte-exact address dump |
19	| Role / ownership along a flow: who does each step? | Text-sketch (flow with a right-column responsibility label) | A separate ownership table detached from the flow |
20	| All-of conditions (AND-intersection): every layer must hold | Text-sketch (funnel / ∩-chain) | Prose list of prerequisites |
21	
22	If two candidate diagrams show the same path, keep the one that answers the more important question. Use a table or boundary note only for exact values or mappings; do not flatten a different process or causal question into rows merely to reduce the diagram count.
23	
24	## Complexity-sensitive visual budget
25	
26	Classify the source before applying a visual count:
27	
28	- **Short or single-mechanism note:** use **1–3 non-duplicative core diagrams** according to distinct supported questions; one diagram is sufficient for a one-question source.
29	- **Long or multi-stage handoff:** let independent reader questions determine the count; **4–7 diagrams is a common range, not a quota**. Keep up to 2–3 core visuals in the one-minute path and move the remaining mechanism, attribution, proof, or decision visuals into deep review.
30	
31	A long source deserves another diagram when it adds a distinct supported layer such as transformation stages, before/after execution shape, resource causality, performance attribution, experiment isolation, or validation closure. It does not deserve another diagram when the candidate only redraws the same arrows with different decoration.
32	
33	For process-heavy technical handoffs, diagrams should normally be at least as numerous as tables. This is a diagnostic, not a scoring rule: pure specifications or lookup-heavy references may correctly use more tables.
34	
35	## Visual-encoding decision (two steps)
36	
37	**Step 1 — diagram or table?** Use a **diagram** when understanding depends on order, causality, branching, state, transformation, layout, parallelism, boundaries, or proof closure. Use a **table** only when the reader compares exact parallel values, fixed properties, file/owner mappings, or compact evidence references. A diagram may point to an exact-value table; the table must not narrate the diagram in row form. Do not pick a table just to stay under a diagram count—choose by information shape, then remove only duplicate visuals. A table that actually encodes a flow, causal chain, layout, or parallelism is a signal to convert it to a diagram.
38	
39	**Step 2 — Mermaid or text-sketch?** Both are canonical.
40	
41	- **Mermaid** for flow / sequence / state / architecture graphs that benefit from rendering and have several branches or participants.
42	- **Text-sketch** (fenced plaintext ASCII) when the point needs precise inline annotation a rendered box cannot hold cleanly (a right-hand "who / effect" column, exact conditions), or is a parallel-lane / SIMD layout, memory/buffer layout, AND-intersection funnel, or a compact state machine—or when platform rendering is unreliable and copy-pasteable monospace is preferable.
43	
44	When the same chain would appear in both an overview / 定位 section and a detailed section, the two must answer **different** reader questions (e.g. ownership / 责任分工 vs data-flow-with-fallback); otherwise keep one.
45	
46	## Construction rules
47	
48	- Give one mechanism or causal chain one primary visual. If a sequence diagram already shows that chain, use a table for its exact timings or evidence; use another diagram only for a different question such as failure lifecycle or experiment validity.
49	- Preserve evidence-backed intermediate states. A start→end summary fails when the omitted transformation or causal steps are necessary to support the conclusion.
50	- Aim for **5–9 semantic nodes** in core diagrams. A deep-review diagram may use up to about **12** when the nodes form one coherent question; otherwise split by phase or question.
51	- Define specialized terms before the first diagram that uses them; label nodes in plain language first, with exact source labels in parentheses when needed.
52	- Use subgraphs only for real component, phase, trust, experiment, or change boundaries.
53	- Add a legend whenever color, line style, symbol, or abbreviation carries meaning. Never rely on color alone; labels must still work in grayscale.
54	- Add at most one takeaway after a diagram when it contributes a boundary, exception, or decision. Omit it when the labels already carry the point.
55	- **No vague, guessed, or unverified label.** A condition, threshold, gate, or step in a visual must be precise and evidence-backed, or marked unknown. Do not invent a plausible-sounding gate to fill a branch (e.g. write "compile-time flag on?" only if the source establishes it; never a filler "size ok?"). A wrong-but-tidy diagram is worse than honest prose.
56	
57	## Compact Mermaid patterns
58	
59	These are generic patterns to adapt, not fixed document templates.
60	
61	### Call flow — position in the system
62	
63	```mermaid
64	flowchart LR
65	    A[Public entry] --> B[Coordinator]
66	    B --> C[Relevant mechanism]
67	    C --> D[Stable dependency]
68	```
69	
70	### Sequence — cross-component interaction
71	
72	```mermaid
73	sequenceDiagram
74	    participant U as Client
75	    participant A as API
76	    participant S as Storage
77	    U->>A: Request operation
78	    A-->>U: Return scoped capability
79	    U->>S: Perform direct transfer
80	    U->>A: Confirm result
81	```
82	
83	If dashed and solid arrows have special meanings beyond Mermaid convention, add an adjacent legend such as `solid = request; dashed = response`.
84	
85	### Decision flow — causal or branching behavior
86	
87	```mermaid
88	flowchart TD
89	    A[Observed input] --> B{Condition met?}
90	    B -->|Yes| C[Primary path]
91	    B -->|No| D[Fallback path]
92	    C --> E[Observable result]
93	    D --> E
94	```
95	
96	### Data flow — transformation stages
97	
98	```mermaid
99	flowchart LR
100	    A[Raw input] --> B[Normalize]
101	    B --> C[Transform in batches]
102	    C --> D[Preserve final semantics]
103	    D --> E[Output]
104	```
105	
106	### Change boundary — changed versus unchanged
107	
108	```mermaid
109	flowchart LR
110	    subgraph Stable[Unchanged behavior]
111	      A[Caller] --> B[Selection logic]
112	    end
113	    subgraph Changed[Changed implementation]
114	      B --> C[Inner operation]
115	    end
116	    C --> D[Same output contract]
117	```
118	
119	### State model — lifecycle
120	
121	```mermaid
122	stateDiagram-v2
123	    [*] --> Pending
124	    Pending --> Complete: success
125	    Pending --> Retry: recoverable failure
126	    Retry --> Complete: later success
127	    Retry --> Failed: retry limit
128	```
129	
130	## Markdown text-sketch (ASCII) patterns
131	
132	A text-sketch is a fenced `plaintext` code block drawn with box/arrow characters (`─ │ ┌ ┐ └ ┘ ▼ ► ◄ ⇄ ∩`). It renders as monospace everywhere, needs no image round-trip, and can carry exact inline annotations that Mermaid boxes cannot hold cleanly.
133	
134	When to reach for it vs Mermaid: see the two-step encoding decision above (text-sketch for precise inline annotation, lanes/layout/funnel/compact state machine, or unreliable rendering; Mermaid for many-branch rendered graphs).
135	
136	**Construction rules**: keep total width modest (it must not overflow the text column); annotate a right-hand column for "who owns it" or "the effect"; one idea per block; CJK characters are double-width, so prioritize readability over pixel-perfect alignment; follow with at most one takeaway.
137	
138	### Pipeline / data-flow with a responsibility column
139	
140	```plaintext
141	输入 ─► 阶段A ─────────────────────────►  (谁管/效果)
142	          │
143	          ▼
144	        阶段B ─────────────────────────►  (谁管/效果)
145	```
146	
147	### Parallel lanes — scalar vs SIMD
148	
149	```plaintext
150	标量 (1 个/拍):  acc += a0·k0 → a1·k1 → ... → aN·kN
151	SIMD (N 个/拍):  [a0 a1 a2 a3]         lane0..3
152	                 [k0 k1 k2 k3]  ┐ 一条指令 = N 个乘加
153	          acc4 += [.. .. .. ..] ┘  收尾: 横向求和
154	```
155	
156	### AND-intersection — every layer must hold
157	
158	```plaintext
159	① 条件A   ─┐
160	② 条件B    ├─ 全部满足 ─► 目标成立
161	③ 条件C   ─┘   任一不满足 ─► 退回/失败   ← 只有"最终实测层"算数
162	```
163	
164	### Memory / buffer layout and reuse
165	
166	```plaintext
167	arena: [ ... | scratch(中间) | ... ]
168	                  │ 用完释放
169	                  ▼
170	       [ ... | 输出 buffer   | ... ]   ← 复用同一区段
171	```
172	
173	### Compact state machine (hysteresis)
174	
175	```plaintext
176	   ┌─────────┐  进入阈值   ┌───────────┐  持续够久 → 记录 start   ┌────────┐
177	   │ 静音    │ ──────────►│ 疑似语音   │ ───────────────────────►│ 语音   │
178	   └─────────┘ ◄────────── └───────────┘ ◄─── 恢复 ───────────── └────────┘
179	        ▲  时长不足回退                         退出阈值 │
180	        └──── 静音够久 → 记录 end ◄─────────────────────┘

21

25	- every independent layer needed for handoff—such as system position, transformation, before/after structure, resource or performance causality, experiment isolation, and validation closure—has a visual or an explicit reason why prose/table is clearer;

31	- a process-heavy handoff that contains more tables than diagrams has been re-checked for flattened processes; a justified specification or lookup-heavy exception is stated by the information shape itself.
32

34	
35	Pass only when:
36	
37	- Each specialized concept first appears as `plain-language meaning → technical term → exact source label`, either inline or in a compact key.
38	- Every acronym is expanded at its first appearance, including titles, conclusions, table cells, and diagram labels.
39	- The terminology key appears before the first sentence or diagram that depends on unfamiliar protocol, request-method, metric, queue, component, or platform terms.
40	- A final top-to-bottom scan finds no definition that occurs after first use.

42	
43	## 3. Claim and diagram provenance
44	
45	For every causal, quantitative, equivalence, or status claim, record or link its provenance.
46	
47	| Claim class | Required provenance or wording |
48	|---|---|
49	| Fact | Source file/diff, log line, measurement, command result, or document block |
50	| Interpretation | Supporting facts plus language such as “indicates” or “therefore” |
51	| Decision | Decision owner or supplied conclusion, rationale, and trade-off when known |
52	| Limit | Untested path, unknown, unavailable evidence, or explicit scope boundary |

55	
56	- rejected hypotheses are not presented as root causes and recommendations are not presented as implemented behavior;
57	- every diagram node, edge, destination, and responsibility maps to supplied evidence or is explicitly labeled as interpretation;
58	- no visual encodes a vague, guessed, or unverified condition, threshold, gate, or step; every branch label is precise and evidence-backed or shown as unknown, and converting prose into a diagram introduced no invented gate;
59	- missing destinations, owners, authorization behavior, deployment state, and lifecycle behavior remain unknown rather than being completed from a typical architecture;
60	- ambiguous source wording is preserved instead of silently choosing one interpretation.
61	
62	## 4. Changed-versus-unchanged boundary
63	
64	Pass only when the document explicitly states:
65	
66	- the smallest behavior or implementation region that changed;
67	- upstream and downstream behavior that stayed unchanged, when supported by the input;
68	- preserved contracts, outputs, failure semantics, or numerical semantics relevant to the conclusion;
69	- configuration or rollout boundaries when supplied.

33	For process-heavy technical handoffs, diagrams should normally be at least as numerous as tables. This is a diagnostic, not a scoring rule: pure specifications or lookup-heavy references may correctly use more tables.

35	## Visual-encoding decision (two steps)

37	**Step 1 — diagram or table?** Use a **diagram** when understanding depends on order, causality, branching, state, transformation, layout, parallelism, boundaries, or proof closure. 48	3. Avoid document-wide overwrite. It can destroy media, whiteboards, comments, and collaborative structure.
49	4. Preserve existing image, file, and whiteboard references/tokens. Do not reconstruct or replace them merely to edit nearby text.
50	5. Keep the selection narrow enough that unrelated blocks cannot be captured.
51	6. If the selection is not unique, refine it or stop; never broaden it speculatively.
52	
53	## Verify after write
54	
55	Re-read the written section and its immediate neighbors. Confirm:
56	
57	- the title, section, and block type still match the intended target;
58	- headings, diagrams, tables, and callouts rendered in the expected order;
59	- existing media and whiteboards remain present;
60	- no adjacent or unrelated content changed;
61	- the final text preserves facts, interpretations, decisions, limits, and source labels from the canonical Markdown.
62	
63	If rendering produced a warning or converted a diagram incorrectly, repair only that block and re-read again. Report the final location and any unresolved rendering limitation.

1	# Readability Gates
2	
3	Run these gates against the canonical Markdown before delivery. A failed gate requires revision or an explicit limit; do not compensate with more prose.
4	
5	## 1. One-minute scanability
6	
7	For every source, pass only when:
8	
9	- The first screen contains a plain-language title, a one-sentence purpose or conclusion, terminology needed by the first visual, and the first useful visual or compact summary.
10	- For a Chinese long-form deep technical document, the reader-facing title uses **“深度梳理”**, not **“交接”** or **“技术交接”**, unless the user supplied an explicit title that must be preserved.
11	- Up to the first **2–3 core diagrams** form an independently scannable path through system position or symptom, main mechanism or cause, change/result boundary, and validation status. A one-question source may pass with one diagram.
12	- Each diagram answers a different reader question.
13	- Optional operations, hardening, and future tests occupy at most a short, clearly labeled follow-up section unless they are part of the requested handoff scope.
14	
15	Apply the numeric budget only after classifying source complexity:
16	
17	- **Short or single-mechanism note:** impose no word-count or diagram minimum. Use **1–3 diagrams** according to distinct supported questions and keep a **900-word ceiling** unless requested depth or evidence preservation requires otherwise. Evidence-rich short notes commonly land around **600–850 words**; tiny one-question inputs should remain substantially shorter.
18	- **Long or multi-stage handoff:** do not apply the short-note word or diagram ceiling. Keep the one-minute path compact and place additional supported mechanism, transformation, attribution, decision, and proof visuals in deep review.
19	
20	## Visual coverage and technical depth
21	
22	For long or multi-stage inputs, pass only when:
23	
24	- the document has an explicit coverage map in the drafting process: `reader question → evidence → visual → exact-value table, if needed → limit`;
25	- every independent layer needed for handoff—such as system position, transformation, before/after structure, resource or performance causality, experiment isolation, and validation closure—has a visual or an explicit reason why prose/table is clearer;
26	- diagrams preserve the evidence-backed intermediate states required to support their conclusions rather than collapsing a multi-stage chain into start→end;
27	- processes, causal chains, state changes, and validation loops are not moved into tables merely because 2–3 diagrams already exist;
28	- tables remain focused on exact comparisons, mappings, or compact evidence lookup;
29	- the first 2–3 diagrams serve the one-minute path while additional diagrams answer distinct deep-review questions;
30	- added length comes from new information layers, exact evidence, boundaries, or decisions—not repeated conclusions, arrow narration, oversized text nodes, or prose padding;
31	- a process-heavy handoff that contains more tables than diagrams has been re-checked for flattened processes; a justified specification or lookup-heavy exception is stated by the information shape itself.
32	
33	## 2. Terminology progression
34	
35	Pass only when:
36	
37	- Each specialized concept first appears as `plain-language meaning → technical term → exact source label`, either inline or in a compact key.
38	- Every acronym is expanded at its first appearance, including titles, conclusions, table cells, and diagram labels.
39	- The terminology key appears before the first sentence or diagram that depends on unfamiliar protocol, request-method, metric, queue, component, or platform terms.
40	- A final top-to-bottom scan finds no definition that occurs after first use.
41	- Every meaningful color, line style, or symbol has a legend, and the diagram remains understandable in grayscale.
42	
43	## 3. Claim and diagram provenance
44	
45	For every causal, quantitative, equivalence, or status claim, record or link its provenance.
46	
47	| Claim class | Required provenance or wording |
48	|---|---|
49	| Fact | Source file/diff, log line, measurement, command result, or document block |
50	| Interpretation | Supporting facts plus language such as “indicates” or “therefore” |
51	| Decision | Decision owner or supplied conclusion, rationale, and trade-off when known |
52	| Limit | Untested path, unknown, unavailable evidence, or explicit scope boundary |
53	
54	Pass only when:
55	
56	- rejected hypotheses are not presented as root causes and recommendations are not presented as implemented behavior;
57	- every diagram node, edge, destination, and responsibility maps to supplied evidence or is explicitly labeled as interpretation;
58	- no visual encodes a vague, guessed, or unverified condition, threshold, gate, or step; every branch label is precise and evidence-backed or shown as unknown, and converting prose into a diagram introduced no invented gate;
59	- missing destinations, owners, authorization behavior, deployment state, and lifecycle behavior remain unknown rather than being completed from a typical architecture;
60	- ambiguous source wording is preserved instead of silently choosing one interpretation.
61	
62	## 4. Changed-versus-unchanged boundary
63	
64	Pass only when the document explicitly states:
65	
66	- the smallest behavior or implementation region that changed;
67	- upstream and downstream behavior that stayed unchanged, when supported by the input;
68	- preserved contracts, outputs, failure semantics, or numerical semantics relevant to the conclusion;
69	- configuration or rollout boundaries when supplied.
70	
71	A changed-file list alone does not pass this gate. If unchanged behavior is not evidenced, label it unknown rather than infer it from silence.
72	
73	## 5. Product, measurement, and validation separation
74	
75	Pass only when each artifact is classified by its supplied role:
76	
77	- **Product:** shipped behavior, implementation, configuration, or runtime path;
78	- **Measurement:** profiling, tracing, logging, counters, or benchmark instrumentation;
79	- **Validation:** tests, fixtures, comparison tools, commands, or expected outputs.
80	
81	Do not infer shipping or deployment status from a path. Do not imply that measurement or validation assets alter product behavior. If one file has multiple roles, identify the relevant section or change rather than assigning one misleading label.
82	
83	## 6. Evidence closure
84	
85	Pass only when:
86	
87	- each conclusion is attributed to the evidence that directly proves it; stronger but indirect evidence is only corroboration;
88	- a negative observation about one branch is not turned into a positive claim that another branch ran unless the alternatives are exhaustive and evidenced;
89	- a tested platform, value, duration, or input is called **tested**, not **supported**;
90	- before/after measurements use comparable conditions, or the mismatch is stated;
91	- a root-cause-removing fix is distinguished from mitigation, containment, or an independent defense;
92	- validation lists completed checks separately from planned or untested checks;
93	- bit-exact, causal, performance, reliability, and security conclusions are not generalized beyond the tested dimensions;
94	- commands and exact values live in deep-review material, not the one-minute path.
95	
96	## 7. Unknowns and limits
97	
98	Pass only when unknowns are visible near the conclusion they constrain. Include untested platforms, configurations, durations, failure modes, dependencies, or operational paths supplied by the evidence. Use **Unknown**, **Untested**, or **Limit** labels; do not hide them in a generic “Notes” section.
99	
100	## 8. Non-duplication and scope
101	
102	Pass only when:
103	
104	- one mechanism or causal chain has one canonical visual;
105	- an overview/定位 diagram and a detailed diagram of the same chain answer different reader questions (e.g. ownership vs data-flow-with-fallback), or are merged into one;
106	- the next section does not recreate that visual as an “at a glance” chronology;
107	- an evidence table maps claims to sources without walking through the same sequence again or repeating every timing value;
108	- prose after a diagram adds evidence, exception, boundary, or decision rather than narrating every arrow;
109	- each key conclusion and quantitative value has one primary home, with at most one short cross-reference when needed;
110	- every section traces to an input fact, supported interpretation, requested decision, or explicitly labeled follow-up;
111	- removing any H2 would lose information needed for the stated goal.
112	
113	## Final self-review
114	
115	- Scan from the title downward for acronyms and specialized nouns whose expansion or explanation appears later; if the conclusion needs them, move the key before the conclusion.
116	- Count whitespace-delimited words for short inputs and trim any result above 900 unless the user requested depth or omission would lose supplied evidence.
117	- Compare every quantitative conclusion with the exact source metric name and scope; reject broadened wording and unsupported superlatives or minimality claims.
118	- For interaction/handoff tasks, confirm one primary visual spans every participant requested by the user without adding unsupplied intermediaries or request payloads.
119	- Search for `TBD`, `TODO`, placeholder labels, invented examples, and unresolved references.
120	- Check each diagram edge against the source notes; remove inferred destinations and responsibilities.
121	- Check Markdown structure and diagram syntax. Both Mermaid diagrams and fenced plaintext text-sketches count as visuals for the one-minute-path and coverage gates; for a text-sketch, confirm it is inside a `plaintext` fence, its width does not overflow the text column, and its nodes/edges still trace to evidence. State a rendering limitation only when rendering was actually attempted and the result matters to the user; do not add unverifiable environment/process notes.
122	- Check that every document link and source reference resolves to the intended evidence or section.
123	- Check terminology and evidence labels for contradictions across summary, diagrams, tables, and limits.
124	- Confirm the canonical Markdown stands alone even when no Feishu adaptation is produced.
